subtopicTitle: Gain margin, phase margin — stability margins

cards.front: What are "stability margins" in the context of control systems?
cards.back: Stability margins quantify how close a control system is to instability. They measure the robustness of a closed-loop system to variations in gain and phase of its open-loop transfer function, $L(s)$. The two primary margins are Gain Margin (GM) and Phase Margin (PM).

cards.front: Define the "phase crossover frequency" ($\omega_{pc}$) for an open-loop transfer function $L(s)$.
cards.back: The phase crossover frequency ($\omega_{pc}$) is the frequency at which the phase angle of the open-loop transfer function $L(j\omega)$ crosses $-180^\circ$. Mathematically, $\angle L(j\omega_{pc}) = -180^\circ$.

cards.front: Given an open-loop transfer function $L(s)$, how is the Gain Margin (GM) calculated and what is its unit?
cards.back: The Gain Margin (GM) is the reciprocal of the magnitude of $L(j\omega)$ at the phase crossover frequency ($\omega_{pc}$). $GM = \frac{1}{|L(j\omega_{pc})|}$. In decibels, $GM_{dB} = -20 \log_{10} |L(j\omega_{pc})|$. It is typically expressed in dB or as a ratio.

cards.front: Define the "gain crossover frequency" ($\omega_{gc}$) for an open-loop transfer function $L(s)$.
cards.back: The gain crossover frequency ($\omega_{gc}$) is the frequency at which the magnitude of the open-loop transfer function $L(j\omega)$ crosses $0 \text{ dB}$ (i.e., $|L(j\omega_{gc})| = 1$).

cards.front: Given an open-loop transfer function $L(s)$, how is the Phase Margin (PM) calculated?
cards.back: The Phase Margin (PM) is the difference between the phase angle of $L(j\omega)$ at the gain crossover frequency ($\omega_{gc}$) and $-180^\circ$. $PM = 180^\circ + \angle L(j\omega_{gc})$. A positive PM indicates stability.

cards.front: Explain the stability implications of a system having positive vs. negative Gain Margin (GM) or Phase Margin (PM).
cards.back:
• GM > 0 dB (or GM > 1 as ratio) AND PM > 0$^{\circ}$: The closed-loop system is stable.
  • GM < 0 dB (or GM < 1 as ratio) OR PM < 0$^{\circ}$: The closed-loop system is unstable.
  • GM = 0 dB (or GM = 1 as ratio) AND PM = 0$^{\circ}$: The closed-loop system is marginally stable (oscillatory).
These margins indicate how much additional gain or phase lag can be tolerated before instability.

cards.front: A control system has insufficient stability margins. What general approaches can be taken to improve both GM and PM?
cards.back:
To improve both Gain Margin (GM) and Phase Margin (PM), common approaches include:
  1. Lead Compensator: Adds phase lead, typically increasing PM and often GM at higher frequencies.
  2. Lag Compensator: Reduces gain at higher frequencies, often increasing GM and sometimes PM, but can reduce bandwidth.
  3. PID Controller Tuning: Adjusting $K_p$, $K_i$, $K_d$ parameters to reshape the open-loop frequency response.
  4. Reducing overall loop gain: While it improves stability, it can degrade steady-state error and transient response.

cards.front: What does it mean if an open-loop transfer function $L(s)$ has no phase crossover frequency ($\omega_{pc}$) or no gain crossover frequency ($\omega_{gc}$)?
cards.back:
• No $\omega_{pc}$ (phase never crosses $-180^\circ$): If $\angle L(j\omega)$ is always greater than $-180^\circ$, GM is infinite, implying unconditional stability with respect to gain variations. If always less than $-180^\circ$, GM is negative infinity, implying instability.
  • No $\omega_{gc}$ (magnitude never crosses $0 \text{ dB}$): If $|L(j\omega)|$ is always less than $0 \text{ dB}$, PM is infinite (unconditionally stable). If always greater than $0 \text{ dB}$, PM is negative infinity (unconditionally unstable).
These indicate very robustly stable or unstable systems.
